edges.description: Intense exercise precipitates fiber breakdown in obscurin-deficient muscle.
The knockout shows the membrane fragility and exercise intolerance proposed to underlie the human disease.
edges.limitations: Frank rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria has not been reported in the mouse. Exercise injury is most marked in the diaphragm, not the limb muscles affected in patients.
Seen in the diaphragm but not the hindlimb muscles of exercised mice.

nodes.description: Very high serum creatine kinase during episodes, with a reported mean over 275,000 IU/L and a maximum of 603,000 IU/L. Creatine kinase can stay raised for days after symptoms improve.

evidence.reference_title: Identification of Compound Heterozygous Variants in OBSCN Gene Associated With Rhabdomyolysis: A Case Report.
evidence.snippet: All patients presented with significant elevation of serum CK (mean value over 275,000 IU/L and maximum up to 603,000 IU/L)

nodes.description: Intense exercise, and sometimes fever, triggers breakdown of obscurin-deficient myofibers. Their contents, including creatine kinase and myoglobin, leak into the blood, producing rhabdomyolysis.

evidence.reference_title: Novel OBSCN variants associated with a risk to exercise-intolerance and rhabdomyolysis.
evidence.snippet: Obscurin-deficient muscle fibers seem to have increased susceptibility to damage triggered by exercise that may lead to rhabdomyolysis.

nodes.description: Under intense mechanical load, obscurin-deficient fibers lose the regular M-band and H-zone structure of the sarcomere. Patient muscle shows myofibrillar disintegration with M- and Z-band disruption and core-like central lesions containing desmin aggregates.

evidence.reference_title: Exercise-induced alterations and loss of sarcomeric M-line organization in the diaphragm muscle of obscurin knockout mice.
evidence.snippet: electron microscopy revealed that, in the diaphragm of exercised obscurin KO mice, but not in the hindlimb muscles, both M-line and H-zone of sarcomeres appeared wavy and less defined

nodes.description: Recurrent, often severe rhabdomyolysis triggered mainly by high-intensity exercise, with onset usually in childhood or the teenage years. One reported patient with biallelic variants had cramps and myalgia without rhabdomyolysis.

nodes.description: There is no OBSCN-directed therapy. Acute episodes are treated as for other causes of rhabdomyolysis, with intravenous fluids and urine alkalinization to protect the kidneys.

nodes.description: Without its obscurin anchor, sAnk1.5 is lost or mislocalized and the longitudinal sarcoplasmic reticulum around the myofibril is disorganized. In patient myoblasts the reticulum holds less calcium than control cells under starvation, which the authors attribute to less efficient calcium re-uptake or storage when metabolism is limited.

nodes.description: Biallelic truncating OBSCN variants reduce the transcript and remove obscurin protein from skeletal muscle. Obscurin normally binds titin and myomesin at the M-band, and through its C-terminus binds the sarcoplasmic reticulum protein sAnk1.5 and ankyrin-B, linking the myofibril to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and to the subsarcolemmal cytoskeleton.

evidence.snippet: We report here that ank1.5, a small splice variant of the ank1 gene localized on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane, is capable of interacting with a sequence of 25 aa located at the COOH terminus of obscurin.

nodes.description: Obscn-null mice have a disorganized longitudinal sarcoplasmic reticulum, mislocalized ankyrin-B and dystrophin, sarcolemmal fragility, reduced running endurance and exercise-induced muscle damage, worst in the diaphragm and with age.

Obscurin targets ankyrin-B to the M-band. Without it, dystrophin is mislocalized at costameres, the subsarcolemmal microtubule network is disrupted, and the sarcolemma becomes fragile, so exercise damages the membrane more than in wild-type muscle. Shown in knockout mice; patient muscle shows reduced ankyrin-1 and ankyrin-2 by proteomics.
